questions.stem: An 84-year-old client is prescribed diphenhydramine. Which age-related adverse-effect concern is most relevant?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Older adults are more susceptible to dizziness, sedation, and hypotension from diphenhydramine, so the prescription warrants caution and safety assessment.","B":"Older adults usually develop less sedation and dizziness from diphenhydramine than younger adults, so age alone reduces concern about adverse effects.","C":"Diphenhydramine improves alertness in older adults despite its antihistamine effects, so it is preferred when allergy treatment must avoid drowsiness.","D":"Diphenhydramine has no age-related precautions for dizziness or blood pressure effects, so routine geriatric medication review is unnecessary when this drug is prescribed."}}
questions.rationale: Diphenhydramine labeling specifically notes that older adults are more likely to experience dizziness, sedation, and hypotension. Option A accurately identifies those age-related safety concerns. Option B incorrectly claims reduced susceptibility. Option C contradicts diphenhydramine's sedating effect. Option D incorrectly denies the geriatric precautions described in the label.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Diphenhydramine Hydrochloride Oral Solution prescribing information
questions.source_detail: Current labeling notes that older adults are more likely to experience dizziness, sedation, and hypotension with diphenhydramine.

questions.stem: A client is starting inhaled fluticasone for maintenance asthma therapy. Which instruction helps reduce a common local adverse effect?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use fluticasone only when acute wheezing begins, because inhaled corticosteroids are intended to provide rapid bronchodilation during an asthma attack.","B":"Swallow water immediately after each dose so medication remaining in the mouth is carried into the stomach and continues the anti-inflammatory effect.","C":"Rinse the mouth with water without swallowing after each inhaled dose to help reduce the risk of oropharyngeal candidiasis from local corticosteroid exposure.","D":"Avoid any valved holding chamber because spacers increase oral drug deposition and therefore increase the risk of candidiasis during inhaled corticosteroid treatment."}}
questions.rationale: Current fluticasone HFA labeling instructs patients to rinse the mouth with water without swallowing after inhalation to reduce the risk of oropharyngeal candidiasis. Option C matches that instruction. Option A misuses a maintenance corticosteroid as a rescue bronchodilator. Option B tells the client to swallow rather than spit the rinse. Option D incorrectly discourages holding-chamber use.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Fluticasone Propionate HFA prescribing information
questions.source_detail: Current labeling instructs patients to rinse the mouth with water without swallowing after inhalation to help reduce the risk of oropharyngeal candidiasis.

questions.stem: A client using an insulin pump develops an unexplained rapid glucose rise. Which safety principle is most important?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An unexplained glucose rise can be observed for several hours before checking the infusion set, because brief pump interruptions rarely cause ketosis.","B":"Infusion-set dislodgement or occlusion can interrupt rapid-acting insulin delivery and lead to ketosis or DKA, so pump problems must be recognized and managed early.","C":"Once pump settings are stable, infusion-set problems are unlikely to alter glucose rapidly because the body maintains a large depot of long-acting insulin.","D":"Pump users can reduce glucose monitoring after the first week of therapy because device malfunction is usually detected before meaningful hyperglycemia or ketosis develops."}}
questions.rationale: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 state that infusion-set dislodgement and occlusion place pump users at risk for ketosis and DKA and must be recognized and managed early; pump education includes troubleshooting. Option B reflects that risk. Option A delays troubleshooting. Option C incorrectly assumes a protective long-acting insulin depot. Option D inappropriately reduces monitoring despite the possibility of device interruption.
questions.source_name: American Diabetes Association — Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026: Diabetes Technology
questions.source_detail: The 2026 Standards state that infusion-set dislodgement or occlusion can place pump users at risk for ketosis and DKA and should be recognized and managed early; pump education includes troubleshooting.

questions.stem: An opioid-naive postoperative client is starting oral morphine. A colleague suggests copying the dose used by a chronically opioid-tolerant patient. Which principle should guide the nurse?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use the chronic opioid-tolerant client's regimen as the starting dose, because prior opioid exposure does not affect how initial morphine dosing should be selected.","B":"Choose a higher initial morphine dose for the opioid-naive client so adequate analgesia is achieved before respiratory status needs to be reassessed.","C":"Delay respiratory monitoring until the second day of therapy, because serious opioid-related respiratory depression is uncommon during treatment initiation.","D":"Individualize the initial morphine regimen, use the lowest dose needed for adequate analgesia, and monitor respiratory status closely during initiation."}}
questions.rationale: Current morphine labeling directs clinicians to individualize the starting regimen, use the lowest dosage necessary for adequate analgesia, and monitor closely for serious respiratory depression, especially during initiation and dose increases. Option D follows those principles. Option A ignores important patient-specific opioid exposure and dosing factors. Option B unnecessarily increases initial exposure. Option C delays monitoring during the period of greatest concern.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Morphine Sulfate Tablets prescribing information
questions.source_detail: Current labeling directs individualized initial dosing, use of the lowest dosage necessary for adequate analgesia, and close monitoring for serious respiratory depression during initiation and dosage increases.
